text: An AI agent reads web pages, emails and tool outputs that anyone can write. Hide one sentence in that text, and the model may follow it instead of its user. This is indirect prompt injection.
The strongest open defense, Meta-SecAlign, keeps untrusted data in its own role, and trains the model to prefer answering the user over obeying the data. It is trained entirely in English.

So what happens when the injection arrives in Hindi? In Urdu script? In Hinglish, Tamil, or Amharic? We built eleven versions of the same attack, each translated, then checked with language identification and back-translation.
We trained Tiny Aya Global, a three-billion-parameter multilingual model, with the Meta-SecAlign recipe, using Lexsi's CuratorKIT, AlignTune, and AuditKIT.

Without the defense, the model obeys the injection in more than half of all cases, in every language. And the standard scorer misses replies that open with bold markdown. It says French is attacked six percent of the time. The real figure is fifty-three.

Now train the defense on English injections only. Attack success falls below nine percent in all eleven variants, including four languages the model never saw in training. The defense learned what data is, not what English is.
But an attacker who tries every language on each case still succeeds one time in five. Averages per language hide this. The real risk is a search across languages.
All of this comes at no cost in utility. So test defenses across languages, report the best-of-all attack, and score replies in a way that survives formatting. Our code, models, and data are open.
